content: In 1839, B. Langenbeck in Germany was the first to identify a yeast-like fungus in human oral infections, specifically in cases of thrush. He also demonstrated that this fungus was the causative agent of thrush. The genus Candida, particularly the species Candida albicans, was later described by botanist Christine Marie Berkhout in her doctoral thesis at the University of Utrecht in 1923. Over time, the classification of this genus and its species has undergone significant changes. Historical names for this genus include Mycotorula and Torulopsis, while Candida albicans was previously referred to as Monilia albicans and Oidium albicans. The current classification of Candida albicans is recognized as nomen conservandum, meaning it is an officially accepted name authorized by the International Botanical Congress (IBC). The genus Candida comprises approximately 150 species, but only a few are known to cause infections in humans. Among these, Candida albicans is the most significant pathogenic species. Other disease-causing species include Candida tropicalis, Candida glabrata, Candida krusei, Candida parapsilosis, Candida dubliniensis, and Candida lusitaniae. Candidiasis can be classified based on the site of infection: 1. Localized mucocutaneous candidiasis: Oropharyngeal candidiasis Esophageal candidiasis Candida vulvovaginitis Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis 2. Invasive candidiasis: Candidaemia Candida endophthalmitis Candida endocarditis Candida osteoarticular disease Pathophysiology: Candida is a normal commensal organism found on the skin and mucous membranes. A healthy immune system and intact, regenerating skin prevent Candida from becoming virulent. The main virulence factors that facilitate infection include: Secretion of molecules that promote adherence to host cells. Production of hydrolytic enzymes, which have a lytic effect on tissues and aid in tissue invasion. Polymorphism: Candida can grow in two forms—pseudohyphae (elongated ellipsoid forms) or yeast (rounded to oval budding forms). While the exact role of polymorphism in virulence is unclear, species capable of causing severe disease often exhibit this ability. Biofilm formation: Candida can form thick biofilms on mucosal surfaces, catheters, and dentures, which enhance its survival and resistance to treatment. Conditions that compromise cell-mediated immunity: T-cell deficiencies, such as in DiGeorge syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, and ataxia-telangiectasia. Bone marrow transplantation Leukemias Use of corticosteroids or immunosuppressive drugs Conditions that worsen general health: Malignancies Recent chemotherapy Trauma Recent surgery Prolonged hospitalization Use of broad-spectrum antibiotics Renal failure Prolonged hemodialysis Devices that promote biofilm formation: Prolonged use of central venous catheters Prolonged use of Foley catheters Prolonged mechanical ventilation Clinical Manifestations: 1. Oropharyngeal candidiasis: Many cases are asymptomatic, especially in mild disease or in patients with poor general health. Symptoms may include dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), odynophagia (painful swallowing), altered taste, and a sensation of fullness or discomfort in the mouth. 2. Candida esophagitis: This condition often occurs late in the course of AIDS or other immunodeficiencies. Symptoms include odynophagia and weight loss due to reduced food intake. 3. Candida vulvovaginitis: Symptoms include intense pruritus (itching), changes in the amount and color of vaginal discharge (characterized by a thick, white, cottage cheese-like discharge), dysuria (painful urination), dyspareunia (pain during sexual intercourse), and vulvovaginal soreness. Symptoms may worsen a week before menstruation. 4. Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMCC): CMCC is a syndrome characterized by chronic or recurrent superficial Candida infections of the skin and mucous membranes, often associated with endocrine and autoimmune deficiencies. It is marked by an inability of T-cells to respond to Candida antigens. Patients may present with recurrent or chronic Candida infections, and endocrinopathies such as hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency may accompany the condition. 5. Invasive candidiasis: Candidaemia: This condition mimics sepsis and presents with high, spiking fevers in immunodeficient patients. Severe cases may involve capillary leak syndrome, leading to edema and third-spacing of fluids. If the respiratory system is the primary source of infection, symptoms may include sore throat, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Candida osteoarticular disease: Bone invasion typically occurs weeks to months after Candidaemia. Fever may not always be present, but patients often experience loss of function, pain, and tenderness in the affected area. Candida endophthalmitis: This condition is seen in severely immunocompromised patients, with intravenous drug abuse being a common risk factor. Fever is not consistently present unless associated with Candidaemia. Symptoms include red eye, floaters, and decreased visual acuity, although significant vision loss usually occurs late in the disease course.
